body.name: Mermaid
body.h1: Mermaid Dot to Dot — Magical 54-Dot Free Printable
body.description: Connect the dots to reveal a beautiful mermaid gliding through the ocean. This easy 54-dot puzzle is perfect for young learners practising number sequencing while enjoying a touch of underwater magic.
body.fun_fact: Mermaids appear in folklore from ancient Syria — over 3,000 years ago!

dot_guide.intro: Mermaids have captured children's imaginations for thousands of years — from the ancient seas of Syria to the fairy tales of Hans Christian Andersen. This beautiful 54-dot puzzle traces the graceful outline of a mermaid gliding through the deep. It is a wonderful puzzle for quiet, focused time — perfect for a rainy afternoon or a calm classroom activity for kids. Find dot 1 and let the magic begin!
dot_guide.outro: Wonderful — your mermaid is ready to dive! Now give her tail the most spectacular colour combination you can imagine. Display it proudly or give it as a gift — either way, you have created something genuinely lovely. Ready for another? Browse more free dot to dot printables to keep the quiet time going.

sections.title: The Face and Hair
sections.learn: Start at dot 1 and connect through to dot 9 to trace the mermaid's face and the flowing lines of her hair. Faces involve gentle, rounded curves — a lovely warm-up that builds pencil confidence before the bigger shapes ahead. Encourage children to lift their wrist slightly and let the pencil glide.
sections.fact: Mermaid legends have appeared independently in cultures all around the world — from West African water spirits to the Japanese Ningyo and the ancient Greek sea-nymph Nereids. The idea of half-human, half-fish beings seems to be something the human imagination keeps arriving at, no matter the ocean.

sections.title: The Arms and Upper Body
sections.learn: Continue from dot 10 to dot 22 to draw the arms and torso. Children practise symmetry and the natural curve of a human figure here — a section that works especially well for discussing body proportions in a fun, low-pressure way. A light, flowing touch gives the most elegant result.
sections.fact: The most famous mermaid story in English-speaking culture — The Little Mermaid — was written by Hans Christian Andersen in 1837. The original tale is quite different from the animated film: far more bittersweet, and intended to reflect on sacrifice, longing, and what it means to have a soul.

sections.title: The Waist and Scales
sections.learn: Trace dots 23 through 36 for the midsection where the human form transitions into the fish tail — the most distinctively mermaid part of the whole drawing. Children learn to follow a shape that narrows and then sweeps outward again. This middle section rewards patience and careful dot-finding.
sections.fact: Scientists believe the mermaid myth may have partly originated from sailors spotting manatees or dugongs at sea. At a distance, a manatee surfacing to breathe — with its rounded body and paddle-like tail — can look surprisingly humanoid. It is a generous interpretation, but loneliness and distance do remarkable things to the imagination.

sections.title: The Fish Tail
sections.learn: Connect dots 37 to 46 to sweep the long, graceful fish tail downward. This is the most satisfying section of the puzzle — children feel the mermaid taking her final, recognisable shape. Long, flowing strokes work beautifully here. Encourage children to draw from the shoulder rather than just the wrist.
sections.fact: In most mermaid folklore, the tail is described as iridescent — shimmering with multiple colours like a soap bubble or a fish scale in sunlight. When it comes to colouring this puzzle, there is no wrong answer: silver, ocean blue, emerald green, or all three at once are all equally valid!

sections.title: The Tail Fins
sections.learn: Finish by connecting dots 47 through 54 to add the broad, sweeping tail fins that complete the mermaid's silhouette. Just eight dots to the finish line — encourage children to make each one count and end with a confident, graceful flourish. The tail fin is the mermaid's full stop!
sections.fact: Fish tails move side-to-side, but whale and dolphin tails — called flukes — move up and down. If a mermaid existed in real life, scientists debate which style of tail would make more sense for a human-shaped upper body. The answer, based on the way human hips move, would likely be the up-and-down dolphin style.

body.name: Merman
body.h1: Merman Dot to Dot for Preschool: 44 Easy Dots, Free
body.description: Connect the dots to reveal a magnificent merman rising from the ocean depths! With 44 easy dots, this puzzle is perfect for preschool and kindergarten children practising number sequencing while exploring underwater fantasy.
body.fun_fact: Male merfolk (mermen) appear in mythology worldwide — from ancient Greece to the Caribbean!

dot_guide.intro: Mermen are the powerful, mysterious kings of the deep ocean — appearing in myths from ancient Greece to the Caribbean, from West Africa to the coastlines of Scotland. Often depicted as fierce rulers of the sea, they are equally at home in quiet lagoons and crashing storms. This 44-dot puzzle is a lovely, manageable challenge for younger children. Grab a pencil and meet the king of the deep!
dot_guide.outro: Brilliant work — your merman is ready to rule the deep! This is a wonderful puzzle to pair with a library visit to find books about ocean mythology. Stories from the sea have been inspiring children's imaginations for thousands of years. Explore more of our dot to dot printables 1-100 from the deep.

sections.title: The Head and Face
sections.learn: Start at dot 1 and connect through to dot 8 to sketch the merman's strong, proud face. This introductory section uses gentle curves and helps children settle into the rhythm of the puzzle. Counting each dot aloud is a great way for parents and caregivers to join in from the very beginning.
sections.fact: In ancient Greek mythology, the sea god Poseidon (Neptune in Roman mythology) was often depicted as a powerful merman-like figure, ruling the oceans with a trident. His son Triton was a full merman — half man, half fish — who could calm or raise storms by blowing on his conch shell trumpet.

sections.title: The Arms and Trident
sections.learn: Continue from dot 9 to dot 18 to draw the outstretched arms and the hint of a trident. Children practise drawing extending shapes that reach outward from the body — a different challenge from drawing shapes that curve inward. This section builds directional awareness and confident outward strokes.
sections.fact: The trident — a three-pronged spear — has been the symbol of sea power in mythology for thousands of years. The word comes from the Latin 'tridens', meaning three teeth. Real-life fishermen across many cultures have used three-pronged spears to catch fish for just as long, so the symbol likely grew from everyday tools.

sections.title: The Powerful Torso
sections.learn: Trace dots 19 through 30 to fill out the broad, muscular torso. This is the longest section of the puzzle and a great opportunity to build sustained concentration — an important classroom and home skill for children aged 4 to 7. Celebrate reaching dot 30 as a milestone halfway through.
sections.fact: Mermen appear in Scottish and Irish folklore as the 'Blue Men of the Minch' — magical sea creatures said to live in the strait between Scotland and the Outer Hebrides. Local storytellers imagined these blue-skinned mermen challenging passing sailors to a poetry competition, and letting the best poets sail safely on!

sections.title: The Fish Tail
sections.learn: Connect dots 31 to 38 to sweep the fish tail into place. Children see the full merman shape emerge in this section — a satisfying moment that rewards all the careful dot-finding that came before. Flowing, confident downward strokes give the tail its natural movement.
sections.fact: The Caribbean sea god Olokun, found in Yoruba mythology originally from West Africa, is a powerful ocean deity sometimes depicted with a fish tail. Olokun represents the depths of the ocean — mysteries, wealth hidden beneath the waves, and the unconscious depths of the human mind. A remarkably poetic image.

sections.title: The Tail Fins
sections.learn: Finish by connecting dots 39 through 44 to add the flowing tail fins. Six dots to complete the king of the deep — encourage children to give these final lines real confidence and sweep. A strong finish is always worth taking a breath for before beginning.
sections.fact: Mermen are sometimes called 'Mermen' or 'Merrows' in Irish folklore, and unlike many mythological sea creatures, they were considered to be generally friendly toward humans — occasionally marrying into fishing families and living on land for a time. The ocean, in these stories, was not a place to fear but a neighbour to respect.

body.name: Seahorse
body.h1: Seahorse Dot to Dot, Our Easiest 35-Dot Ocean PDF
body.description: Connect the dots to reveal a charming seahorse floating through the sea! With just 35 easy dots, this puzzle is ideal for preschool and kindergarten children building number sequencing skills with an adorable ocean friend.
body.fun_fact: Seahorses are the only fish where the male carries and gives birth to the babies!

dot_guide.intro: The seahorse is one of the most extraordinary creatures in the entire ocean — not just for how it looks, but for how it lives. It swims upright, it moves by flickering a tiny fin on its back, it anchors itself to seaweed with its curling tail, and the father is the one who carries and gives birth to the babies. If you were designing an animal from scratch, you would never imagine something this wonderfully unusual. Let's draw one together!
dot_guide.outro: Lovely work — your seahorse is complete! Did you know seahorses come in over 45 different species, in colours ranging from bright yellow to deep purple to almost completely transparent? Colour yours however you like — in the seahorse world, anything goes. Looking for your next challenge? Browse all our dot to dot printables.

sections.title: The Head and Snout
sections.learn: Start at dot 1 and connect through to dot 6 to draw the seahorse's distinctive horse-like head and long, tube-shaped snout. This tiny section is a lovely, manageable start for younger children — just six dots to build confidence before the bigger sections ahead. The snout is one of the most unusual shapes in the animal kingdom.
sections.fact: A seahorse has no teeth and no stomach. It sucks in tiny shrimp and plankton through its snout like a vacuum cleaner, and because food passes through so quickly, it must eat almost constantly — up to 3,000 brine shrimp per day. Being a seahorse is essentially a full-time eating job.

sections.title: The Curved Neck and Mane
sections.learn: Continue from dot 7 to dot 16 to trace the beautifully curved neck and the ridge along the back — sometimes called the seahorse's mane. This section has the loveliest curve in the whole puzzle. Children learn to follow a long, smooth arc, keeping their pencil moving slowly and evenly for the best result.
sections.fact: Seahorses are genuinely one of the slowest fish in the ocean, moving at a top speed of about five feet per hour. To put that in perspective, a garden snail moves faster. Rather than chasing prey, the seahorse relies entirely on camouflage and surprise — drifting close to food and then striking with lightning speed.

sections.title: The Body Rings
sections.learn: Trace dots 17 through 26 to draw the distinctively segmented body — those raised bony rings that run from neck to tail. Children learn here that animal bodies are not always smooth, and begin to notice the beautiful structure of the seahorse's natural armour. This section rewards careful, deliberate dot-following.
sections.fact: A seahorse is not covered in scales like most fish — instead its body is encased in bony plates arranged in rings. This makes it quite rigid, which is why it cannot wriggle like most fish. It is essentially wearing a suit of armour, which also makes it one of the toughest small creatures in the sea for a predator to swallow.

sections.title: The Curling Tail
sections.learn: Finish the puzzle by connecting dots 27 through 35 to draw the long, curling tail that sweeps beneath the body. The tail is one of the most satisfying shapes to draw — children practise a tight, diminishing spiral that is both challenging and deeply rewarding. Nine dots to the finish!
sections.fact: The seahorse tail is prehensile — meaning it can grip things, just like a monkey's tail. Seahorses anchor themselves to coral and seaweed with their tails to avoid being swept away by currents. During mating, a male and female will wrap their tails together and drift through the water side by side — one of the most romantic sights in the ocean.

body.name: Whale
body.h1: Whale Dot to Dot Printable — 42 Easy Dots to Join
body.tagline: A Gentle Giant of the Sea
body.description: Connect 42 easy dots to reveal a magnificent whale swimming through the ocean. This printable puzzle helps preschool and kindergarten children practise number sequencing, pencil control, and concentration.
body.fun_fact: Blue whales are the largest animals known to have ever lived on Earth!

dot_guide.intro: The whale is the largest animal that has ever existed on our planet — bigger than any dinosaur, bigger than anything that has ever lived on land. And yet, for all their enormous size, whales are gentle, intelligent, deeply social creatures that sing to one another across hundreds of miles of open ocean. This 42-dot puzzle captures that peaceful, unhurried quality. Take a deep breath, find dot 1, and dive in!
dot_guide.outro: You have just drawn the largest animal on Earth — well done! This puzzle pairs beautifully with a conversation about ocean conservation. Whales were hunted almost to extinction last century and are now slowly recovering. Children who love whales today are exactly the kind of people who will protect them tomorrow. For more classroom-ready pages, see our dot to dot worksheets.

sections.title: The Head and Mouth
sections.learn: Start at dot 1 and connect through to dot 8 to draw the whale's broad, rounded head and the gentle curve of the mouth. Whales have some of the most peacefully shaped heads in nature — no sharp teeth visible, no fierce expression. Children practise wide, slow curves here, matching the whale's own unhurried character.
sections.fact: A blue whale's heart is about the size of a small car — roughly 400 pounds — and beats only around 8 to 10 times per minute when the whale is diving. When it surfaces, the heart speeds up to 25–37 beats per minute. It is the largest heart of any animal ever known to exist on Earth — truly incredible!

sections.title: The Back and Dorsal Fin
sections.learn: Continue from dot 9 to dot 18 to trace the long, smooth back and the small dorsal fin. Compared to a dolphin's tall fin, a blue whale's dorsal fin is tiny — children often comment on this, which sparks a lovely discussion about why different animals have different features. Long, flowing strokes work best for this gentle curve.
sections.fact: Whale skin carries unique patterns of scars, spots, and markings — so distinctive that scientists can identify individual whales from photographs alone. Some whales in long-running studies have been followed for over 30 years. We know individual whales by name, personality, and family history. That is a remarkable thing.

sections.title: The Belly and Body
sections.learn: Trace dots 19 through 30 to fill out the enormous belly and complete the main body shape. The whale's underside is often a lighter colour than the back — a form of camouflage called countershading, common in ocean animals. Children practise the longest section of the puzzle here, building real concentration stamina.
sections.fact: A blue whale can eat up to four tonnes of krill — tiny shrimp-like creatures — in a single day. It does this by lunging into a swarm with its mouth open, gulping an enormous quantity of water, then pushing the water out through plates of baleen while the krill stays trapped inside. An elegant, ancient technique.

sections.title: The Flippers
sections.learn: Connect dots 31 to 36 to draw the long, paddle-shaped flippers. Whale flippers contain the same bones as a human hand and arm — five finger bones, a wrist, and an upper arm — just reshaped over millions of years for life in the ocean. Children love discovering this when you point it out mid-puzzle.
sections.fact: Inside a whale flipper are the same bones you have in your own hand — thumb, fingers, wrist, and all. Whales' ancestors walked on land around 50 million years ago, and the flipper is what those legs became over time. Evolution is essentially a very slow, very patient sculptor.

sections.title: The Tail Flukes
sections.learn: Finish the puzzle by connecting dots 37 through 42 to draw the broad tail flukes — the most powerful structure in the animal kingdom relative to its purpose. Just six dots to complete this gentle giant. Encourage a confident, sweeping finish: the whale deserves a grand conclusion.
sections.fact: A blue whale's tail flukes can be up to 25 feet wide — wider than many houses. Each downward stroke of those flukes propels the whale forward at up to 20 miles per hour in short bursts. Whale song — produced without any vocal cords — can travel over 1,000 miles through deep ocean water. These animals are extraordinary in almost every imaginable way.

body.name: Jellyfish
body.h1: Jellyfish Dot to Dot: an 88-Dot Step-Up Printable
body.description: Connect 88 dots to reveal a graceful jellyfish drifting through the sea. This slightly bigger puzzle is a great step up for children aged 6-9 who are ready for extra dots and more detailed number sequencing practice.
body.fun_fact: Jellyfish have no brain, no heart, and no bones — yet they have survived for over 500 million years!

dot_guide.intro: Jellyfish are among the strangest and most ancient animals in the ocean — they were drifting through the seas long before dinosaurs ever walked the earth, and long before fish, or even bones, existed. With no brain, no heart, and no blood, they are living proof that nature does not need complexity to succeed. This 88-dot puzzle is a satisfying step up for older children ready for a bigger challenge. Find dot 1 and let's start drifting!
dot_guide.outro: Wonderful work — your jellyfish is ready to drift! This puzzle pairs nicely with a conversation about how some of the oldest animals on Earth are also some of the simplest. Colour your jellyfish in translucent blues, purples, or pinks for a realistic glow, or go bold and bright — either way, it will look stunning. Ready for your next challenge? Browse more dot to dot printables 1-100 from the deep.

sections.title: The Bell
sections.learn: Start at dot 1 and connect through to dot 18 to trace the rounded, dome-shaped bell — the jellyfish's main body. This is the largest section of the puzzle, and a great chance to practise smooth, wide curves without lifting the pencil. Encourage slow, steady strokes to keep the dome's shape nice and even.
sections.fact: The jellyfish's bell is not just a body shape — it is also how the animal moves. By contracting and relaxing the bell like a pulsing umbrella, a jellyfish pushes water out behind it and propels itself forward. It is one of the oldest and simplest forms of movement in the animal kingdom, and it still works beautifully 500 million years later.

sections.title: The Fringe and Frills
sections.learn: Continue from dot 19 to dot 40 to draw the ruffled, frilly edge around the base of the bell. This section has lots of small curves close together, which is great practice for careful, patient dot-finding — a good challenge for children moving beyond the easiest puzzles.
sections.fact: Some jellyfish species can produce their own light through a chemical reaction called bioluminescence. In the deep, dark ocean, a glowing jellyfish can look like a floating lantern — a beautiful way to either attract prey or startle a predator, depending on the species.

sections.title: The Trailing Tentacles
sections.learn: Trace dots 41 through 62 to draw the long, trailing tentacles that drift beneath the bell. These lines are longer and looser than the earlier sections, so encourage children to draw them with a relaxed hand, almost as if the pencil itself is floating in water.
sections.fact: The tentacles of a box jellyfish carry some of the most powerful venom in the entire animal kingdom, used to instantly stun small fish and shrimp. Most jellyfish, however, are harmless to humans — only a small handful of species can deliver a sting that people need to worry about.

sections.title: The Oral Arms
sections.learn: Connect dots 63 to 80 to add the shorter, frillier oral arms near the centre of the jellyfish, which help guide food toward its mouth. This section rewards close attention, since the lines sit near each other. A slower pace here leads to the cleanest results.
sections.fact: Jellyfish do not have a mouth and a separate exit — food goes in and waste comes out through the very same opening. It might sound unusual, but it is a wonderfully efficient design that has needed no upgrades in half a billion years.

sections.title: The Final Trailing Threads
sections.learn: Finish the puzzle by connecting dots 81 through 88 to complete the last few drifting threads beneath the tentacles. Just eight dots to the finish line — a calm, gentle way to complete a bigger puzzle. Take a breath and let the final lines drift naturally into place.
sections.fact: Jellyfish are found in every ocean on Earth, from the warm surface waters near the equator to the freezing depths near the poles. Some species have even been found more than 12,000 feet below the surface, drifting silently in complete darkness.

dot_guide.heading: How to Solve the Great White Shark Dot-to-Dot Puzzle
dot_guide.intro: The great white shark is one of the ocean's most famous and most misunderstood animals — a powerful, streamlined hunter that has patrolled the seas for millions of years. This 64-dot puzzle is our trickiest ocean challenge yet, with more dots than the mermaid, whale, or merman, making it a satisfying step up for children ready for extra practice. Find dot 1 and let's meet the ocean's greatest hunter!
dot_guide.outro: Incredible work—your great white shark is ready to patrol the ocean! Colour it in classic ocean grey and white, then add some bubbles and a school of smaller fish nearby. Try the whale dot to dot puzzle next for another exciting ocean adventure.

sections.title: The Snout and Jaws
sections.learn: Start at dot 1 and connect through to dot 13 to draw the shark's pointed snout and powerful jaw line. This is the most recognisable part of the shark, so encourage children to take their time and follow each dot carefully to get that classic, streamlined shape.
sections.fact: A great white shark can have up to 300 teeth arranged in several rows at once. When a tooth breaks or falls out, a new one simply moves forward to replace it — sharks can go through tens of thousands of teeth in a lifetime!

sections.title: The Dorsal Fin
sections.learn: Continue from dot 14 to dot 26 to shape the tall, triangular dorsal fin on the shark's back — the famous fin that breaks the surface of the water.
sections.fact: A shark's dorsal fin helps keep it stable and stops it from rolling side to side while it swims.

sections.title: The Streamlined Body
sections.learn: Follow dots 27 through 40 along the long, powerful body that lets the shark glide smoothly through the water.
sections.fact: A great white's torpedo-shaped body can reach lengths of up to 20 feet — longer than a school bus lane!

sections.title: The Pectoral Fins
sections.learn: Trace dots 41 through 52 to add the wide pectoral fins near the front of the body, used for steering.
sections.fact: Pectoral fins act like the wings of a plane, letting the shark steer up, down, left, and right as it swims.

sections.title: The Tail Fin and Finish
sections.learn: Finish with dots 53 through 64 to complete the powerful, crescent-shaped tail fin that pushes the shark forward.
sections.fact: A great white's tail beats side to side to power it through the water at bursts of up to 25 miles per hour.

body.description: Connect 81 numbered dots to reveal a long, curving electric eel. This medium-level printable helps children practise number sequencing, concentration, and pencil control while discovering one of South America's most remarkable fish.
body.fun_fact: Electric eels can produce powerful electrical pulses to find prey, defend themselves, and sense their surroundings in murky water.

dot_guide.heading: How to Complete the Electric Eel Dot to Dot
dot_guide.intro: Electric eels live in slow-moving freshwater rivers and flooded forests in South America. Although their name says eel, they are actually a type of knifefish. Begin at dot 1 near the top of the head, then follow the numbers carefully as the body curves across the page.
dot_guide.outro: Excellent work — your electric eel is complete! Add deep olive, golden brown, or charcoal colors, then draw ripples around its long body to create a muddy Amazon river habitat. Explore more ocean and water-animal dot to dot printables for another challenge.

sections.title: Across the Upper Body
sections.learn: Start at dot 1 and connect through dot 18 to trace the smooth upper edge of the eel. The wide spacing encourages steady, controlled strokes while children practise finding two-digit numbers in order.
sections.fact: Electric eels breathe air at the water's surface because their oxygen-poor river habitats do not provide enough oxygen through the gills alone.

sections.title: Around the Tail
sections.learn: Continue from dot 19 through dot 38 around the narrow tail and lower curve. Watch each turn closely and keep the line moving from one numbered point to the next.
sections.fact: Most of an electric eel's long body contains specialized organs that generate and control electrical pulses.

sections.title: Along the Lower Body
sections.learn: Connect dots 39 to 54 along the underside of the eel. This section combines gentle curves with shorter steps, building pencil control and visual tracking.
sections.fact: An electric eel swims by rippling a long fin along the underside of its body, allowing it to move forward or backward with surprising precision.

sections.title: Back Toward the Head
sections.learn: Follow dots 55 through 70 as the line travels back toward the head. Check each number before drawing so the eel's rounded body stays smooth and recognizable.
sections.fact: Weak electrical pulses help electric eels navigate and detect nearby objects in dark, muddy water, working a little like an electric sense.

sections.title: Complete the Face
sections.learn: Finish with dots 71 through 81 to close the outline around the face and forehead. These final eleven dots reward careful counting and complete the eel's expressive profile.
sections.fact: Electric eels have poor eyesight, so their electrical sensing system is especially useful for understanding what is around them.
